newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Bachelors ball taps myth about lonely Alaska men.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Bachelors ball taps myth about lonely Alaska men.

text.p: Outside, the snow fell steadily and the temperature dipped below freezing. Inside, one of the self-described lonely bachelors pranced around the barroom in nothing but a handsewn fur G-string, trying to spark romance in the crowd of women who had come from as far away as New York to view the spectacle.

Welcome to the Talkeetna Bachelor Ball, an annual ritual that attemps to lure women in the dead of winter to this tiny town of 330 at the base of Mount McKinley. Although it was sometimes hard to tell where self-parody ended and sincere courtship began, the unattached men hosting the Saturday night event claim the scarcity of eligible women in this corner of Alaska is no laughing matter.

That was whole reason why the Bachelor Ball started 16 years ago, Dick Schmitz, a former president of the Talkeetna Bachelor Society, said. The 50ish bachelor recalled that local men were sitting around at a bar one winter day complaining about the lack of companionship. "They said, 'We've got to do something. There's no women in the town.'"
And, said 29-year-old Skip Evans, women from the Lower 48 who are bored with nine-to-five yuppies who "don't have a rat's a-- about what's going on" should consider seeking their partners here.

"A lot of women out there would like to come to Alaska. They want to meet the man who's going to turn them around, then get them going in the right direction," Evans, a part-time commercial fisherman, said in an Arkansas drawl still thick despite his 10 years in the far north.

In truth, there is no great dearth of women in Alaska. The last time there was one may have been during the Gold Rush in the late 19th century, state demographer Greg Williams said. Alaska has 108 men to every 100 women, he said. The scarcity of elderly residents and abundance of military personnel tilts the gender ratio slightly toward men, but not overwhelmingly.

"It is not in any way really substantially out of whack," Williams said. So why the myths about crowds of mate-seeking Alaskan men? "There's a lot of lonely people around the country who are looking for someone and there's a lot of people willing to exploit that," he said.

Indeed, the lonelyhearts mystique has become a booming industry. A nationally circulated magazine, AlaskaMen, offers biographical sketches, photographs, addresses and telephone numbers of eligible males. A copycat publication sprang up with names and photographs of Florida women interested in forming attachments with supposedly isolated Alaska men.
SOME WOMEN BUY INTO THE MYTH

Special singles tours draw crowds of women to Alaska each summer. And personal notices in the Anchorage Daily News each week include several appeals from non-Alaska women who advertise that they are "willing to relocate."

"Alaska has the sense of romance, adventure, mystery, magical difference," said Pat Walsh, a Fairbanks woman and co-author of "Catch and Release," a new tongue-in-cheek guide to Alaska men. But women seeking Mr. Right might be advised to lower their standards, according to the book, which portrays many Alaska men as unwashed deadbeats.
The book's cover quotes the well-worn slogan about Alaska men: "The odds are good, but the goods are odd."

As Saturday night turned into Sunday morning, some Talkeetna bachelors conceded that many of them were probably doomed to singledom. "We want to be hunting and fishing and do barroom games. It might be because we're lonely," said Tony Christianson, a 51-year-old oil-field maintenance supervisor. "We don't want commitment. We want to be bachelors. That's the truth. We want to be free spirits."

And the women at the Bachelors Ball said they were less interested in finding mates than in aiding other women. Proceeds from an "auction" were earmarked for an Anchorage women's centre that operates a shelter and other services.
Bids -- as high as $150 for a guitar-playing local pilot -- won a drink and a dance with a bachelor of the woman's choice.
"The joke is whether they have teeth or not," said one Anchorage woman, who asked that her name not be used. "I'm not here to find a boyfriend or a husband. I'm here because it's a charity."
